fireworks.e: From fire + work(s). The similarity with Dutch vuurwerk and German Feuerwerk, both “fireworks”, is hardly coincidental.
fireworks.x: 5000 Marrons in Battery, which continue firing to the End of the Fireworks.

firmament.e: From Middle English firmament, furmament (“heaven; sky”), from Old French firmament (“firmament”), or from its etymon Latin firmāmentum (“support.
firmament.x: And thei that be wiſe, ſhal ſhine, as the brightnes of the firmament: & they that turne to righteouſnes, ſhal ſhine as the ſtarres, for euer and euer.

firmly.e: From Middle English fermely; equivalent to firm + -ly.
firmly.x: She corrected him firmly but gently.

firmness.x: France, for the first time since the death of Charlemagne, was governed by a prince of great firmness and ability.

firstly.e: Coined before 1475, from Middle English fyrst-lyk, equivalent to first + -ly.

fiscal.e: From Middle French fiscal, from Latin fiscus (“treasury”) – see fiscus and fisc.
fiscal.x: The allotment is $22 million less than the Pentagon spent on military bands in fiscal 1990.

fisher.e: From Middle English fischer, fischare, from Old English fisċere (“fisher”), from Proto-Germanic *fiskārijaz (“fisher”), equivalent to fish + -er.
fisher.x: The fishers who live here left for the mainland only days ago as an unseasonable October storm ravaged the islands.

fisherman.x: He is a fisherman, out on a trawler for days at a time.

fishery.x: This fishery, which at its peak produced more than 80,000 tons a year, is now in decline.

fishhook.e: From Middle English fisch-hook, from Old English *fischōc (“fishhook”), equivalent to fish + hook. Cognate with Dutch vishaak (“fishhook”).
fishhook.x: Others sprint off and take position — their jackal ears fully erect, their fishhook tails twitching like flags in a stiff wind.

fishmonger.e: From Middle English fisshemonger; equivalent to fish + monger.

fission.e: Borrowed from Latin fissiōnem, accusative singular of fissiō (“the act of breaking up”), from findō (“split, divide”).

fistula.e: Learned borrowing from Latin fistula (“pipe, ulcer, catheter”). Doublet of fester.
fistula.x: An intestinal fistula is an unwanted pathway from intestines to other organs (e.g., the bladder).

fitness.e: From fit + -ness. First attested in the 16th century, with the physical sense from 1935.

fitting.e: From fit (“to conform to in shape or size; to be suitable for”, verb) + -ing (suffix forming present participles of verbs, and gerunds and nouns denoting the act of doing…
fitting.x: O my ſvveet ſir, nevves fitting to the night, / Blacke, fearefull, comfortleſſe, and horrible.

fivefold.e: From Middle English fiffold, from Old English fīffeald. Equivalent to five + -fold.

fixation.e: From Old French fixation. By surface analysis, fix + -ation.
fixation.x: In order to obtain copyright on a recording in the United States, the recording must have been reduced to fixation on or after February 15, 1972.

flabby.e: From a variant of flappy, from flap (“to hang loose”). Compare English dialectal flapsy (“flabby”), Middle Dutch flabbe (“a slap in the face; a fan-blade; a hair ribbon.
flabby.x: A neglected gap was all the gate it had, and the first glance at the place was enough to let you see the flabby devil was running that show.

flaccid.x: The flaccid economy of the 1970s rendered Americans even more hostile toward liberal welfare policies.

flagrant.e: From Middle French flagrant, from Latin flagrantem, present participle of flagrare (“blaze, burn”). More at black.

flagship.x: After Russia’s flagship in the Black Sea, the Moskva, sank last week, the authorities said that the entire crew of more than 500 had been rescued.

flagstone.x: Grass sprouted between the pebbles and a greenish stain lay upon the flagstones.

flail.x: On him alone the curse of Cain Fell, like a flail on the garnered grain, And struck him to the earth!

flair.e: From Middle English flayre, from Old French flair (“scent, odour”), from flairier (“to reek, smell”), from Latin flāgrō, dissimilated variation of frāgrō (“emit a sweet…
flair.x: Each writer offers a unique flair to readers.

flaky.x: I cannot enjoy the online game because of my flaky Internet connection.

flamenco.e: Borrowed from Spanish flamenco, from Middle Dutch vlaminc (“Fleming”) (> Dutch Vlaming).

flamethrower.e: From flame + thrower, calque of German Flammenwerfer.

flaming.x: The flaming debris kept the firefighter well back, and the sparks threatened the neighborhood.

flamingo.e: From Portuguese flamengo (“flamingo”) and Spanish flamenco (“flamingo”), which were adapted from Catalan flamenc (“flamingo”), of disputed ultimate origin in this sense.

flammable.e: Back-formation from inflammable, which is used to avoid confusion with non-flammable, as the prefix in- is often used to mean "un-.
flammable.x: With her play Diamond Lil, she discovered a way to sneak her flammable subject matter past the censors.

flange.e: From dialectal English flange (“to project”), flanch (“a projection”), from Middle French flanche, from Old French flanche (“flank, side”), from Frankish *hlanku (“bend…

flank.x: Stately colonnades are flank'd with trees.

flare.e: Origin uncertain, first recorded in the mid 16th century, probably related to Latin flagrō (“to burn”). Norwegian flara (“to blaze.
flare.x: Flares were used to steer the traffic away from the accident.

flashback.x: Maude Lebowski: What do you do for recreation? / The Dude: Oh, the usual. I bowl. Drive around. The occasional acid flashback.

flashlight.x: I shone my flashlight on the strange inscription.

flatmate.x: One night, one of the flatmates (the one who owned the house) was ranting and raving all night about her girlfriend.

flatten.x: As there was a lot of damage, we chose the heavy roller to flatten the pitch.

flatter.x: Before the results came out, I flattered myself that I had done well on the test. It turned out I was the worst in the class!

flatterer.e: From Middle English flaterere, equivalent to flatter + -er.

flattery.e: From Middle English flaterye, flaterie, from Old French flaterie, from the verb flater (“to flatter”). By surface analysis, flatter + -y (forming abstract nouns).
flattery.x: Don't you know that some of his contributions here are pure flattery?

flatulence.e: From French flatulence, ultimately from Latin flō (“breathe, blow”).

flatulent.x: Sorry, I'm a bit flatulent at the moment - just eaten some curry.

flatworm.e: From flat + worm, a calque of taxonomic name Platyhelminthes.

flaunt.e: Of North Germanic origin. Perhaps related to Norwegian flanta (“to show off, wander about”), Icelandic flana (“to rush about, act rashly or heedlessly”) and then also to…
flaunt.x: She’s always flaunting her designer clothes.

flautist.x: The flautist Bezaly adds to the impressive list of flute concertos dedicated to her with the composer Pulkkis’s contribution to the genre.

flavor.x: The flavor of this apple pie is delicious.

flavoring.x: This soda has an aftertaste because of the artificial flavoring.

flawless.x: The pianist’s performance this evening was flawless.

flaxen.e: From Middle English flaxen, flexon, flexin, from Old English fleaxen (“of flax; flaxen”), equivalent to flax + -en (“made of”). Compare Dutch vlassen.
flaxen.x: The couple and their children have flaxen hair.

fleece.e: From Middle English fles, flees, flese, from Old English flēos, flīes, flȳs, from Proto-West Germanic *fleus.

fleeting.e: From Middle English fleten (“to float”), from Old English flēotan (“to float”), from Proto-Germanic *fleutaną, from Proto-Indo-European *plewd-.
fleeting.x: And I am inspired afresh to pursue the stunning beauty of Christ rather than the fleeting beauty of this world.

fleshy.e: From Middle English fleisshy, fleischy, fleschi, equivalent to flesh + -y. Piecewise doublet of fleischig.
fleshy.x: The King's face was slightly more fleshy than mine, the oval of its contour the least trifle more pronounced.

flexibility.e: From French flexibilité, from Late Latin flexibilitās, from Latin flectō (“to bend, curve”). Equivalent to flexible + -ity = flex + -ibility.
flexibility.x: I had some flexibility in terms of whether to stay in a hotel or in a bed-and-breakfast.

flexible.e: From Middle French flexible, from Latin flexibilis, from flectō (“to bend, curve”). Morphologically flex + -ible.
flexible.x: When the splitting wind Makes flexible the knees of knotted oaks.

flexor.e: From New Latin flexor, agent noun of flectō (“to bend”).

flick.e: From Middle English flykke (“light blow or stroke”). Later uses apparently interpreted as a back-formation from flicker.
flick.x: He removed the speck of dust with a flick of his finger.

flightless.x: The indigenous fauna of Australia and New Zealand featured an especially interesting array of flightless birds.

flighty.e: From flight + -y. Compare Dutch vluchtig (“volatile; fleeting; cursory”), German flüchtig (“volatile; fleeting; momentary; quick”), Danish flygtig (“elusive.

flinch.e: From Middle French flenchir (“to bend”), from Old French flenchir, flanchir, from Frankish *hlankijan, from Proto-Germanic *hlankijaną (“to bend, twist, flex”), from…
flinch.x: My eye doctor hates the flinch I have every time he tries to get near my eyes.

fling.e: From Middle English fling, from the verb (see below). Compare Icelandic flengur (“a fast sprint”).
fling.x: When I was as young as you, I had my fling. I led a life of pleasure.

flint.x: In a cornfield on one side flakings of flint are numerous.

flippant.e: 1595, from Northern English dialectal flippand (“prattling, babbling, glib”), present participle of flip (“to babble”), of North Germanic origin.
flippant.x: The conversations had grown more adult over the years—she was less flippant, at least.

flipper.e: From flip + -er. Compare Saterland Frisian Flappert (“flipper, wing”).
flipper.x: When standing alone, a flat may have a small extension, a FLIPPER, for added strength.

flirtatious.x: It as not for him to stroll past the groups of watchful girls, blowing a flute made of an eagle's wing bone, as the flirtatious young bucks did.

float.x: Helium balloons float in air, while air-filled balloons don't.

flock.e: From Middle English flok (“tuft of wool”), from Old French floc (“tuft of wool”), from Late Latin floccus (“tuft of wool”), probably from Frankish *flokko (“down, wool…
flock.x: I prythee, Tom, beat Cut's saddle, put a few flocks in the point.

flood.x: There is a tide in the affairs of men, / Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune.

floorboard.x: The officers said they found two rifles in the car, one on the front floorboard of the vehicle and another on the rear floorboard.

flooring.x: Every day we are exposed to low doses of phthalates in food containers, perfumes, hairsprays, floorings, paints, toys and medical devices.

flora.x: Thirdly, I continue to attempt to interdigitate the taxa in our flora with taxa of the remainder of the world.

floral.e: From French floral, from Latin flōrālis, from flōs (“flower”).
floral.x: Really, I like the floral pattern on this Chinese vase.

florist.e: From French fleuriste, from Latin floris (“genitive singular of flōs, flower”), + -ist.
florist.x: “After the gown, we can go to the florist, then stop by the lingerie store.”

flotation.x: This week's SpaceX flotation is just the latest sign: we are facing regime change not just in technology, but in finance.

flotilla.e: From Spanish flotilla, diminutive of flota (“fleet”), from French flotte.
flotilla.x: After a few moments Chloe saw Rosamund walking towards them with a small flotilla of shopping bags.

flotsam.e: From Anglo-Norman floteson, from Old French flotaison (“a floating”), from floter (“to float”), of Germanic origin (See float.), + -aison, from Latin -atio.
flotsam.x: STORAGE boxes -- catchalls for flotsam, jetsam, whatnots and thingamajigs -- are gaining new interest as decorative objects for the home.

flounder.e: From Middle English flowndre, from Anglo-Norman floundre, from Old Northern French flondre, from Old Norse flyðra, from Proto-Germanic *flunþrijǭ.

flour.e: Spelled (until about 1830) and meaning flower in the sense of flour being the "finest portion of ground grain" (compare French fleur de farine, fine fleur).

flourish.e: From Middle English floryschen, from Old French florir (via the arrhizotonic stem floriss-), from Late Latin flōrīre, from Latin flōrēre, from Latin flōrem (“flower”…
flourish.x: The barley flourished in the warm weather.

floury.e: From Middle English floury, equivalent to flour + -y. Piecewise doublet of flowery.
floury.x: These mashed potatoes have a floury texture.

flowerpot.x: As a multifaceted kitchen enabler, nothing can quite supplant the gorgeous, timeless, ever-available, often dirt-cheap terra-cotta flowerpot.

fluctuation.e: Borrowed from Latin fluctuatiōnem, accusative singular of fluctuatiō, from fluctuō, from fluctus. Morphologically fluctuate + -ion.
fluctuation.x: The rolling stock has been specially designed to meet the needs of the fluctuation of traffic in peak and off-peak periods.

fluency.e: From Late Latin fluentia, equivalent to fluent + -cy. Cognate with French fluence.
fluency.x: She has fluency, nobility, / Elegance and symmetry, / Stability, fluidity, / Like poetry in motion.

fluently.x: He lived in Mexico, so he is able to speak Spanish fluently.

fluff.e: From earlier floow (“woolly substance, down, nap, lint”), also spelt flough, flue, and flew, from West Flemish vluwe, of uncertain ultimate origin: * Compare Old English…
fluff.x: That article was basically a bunch of fluff. It didn't say anything substantive.

fluffy.x: Fluffy bunny rabbits are really nice to stroke.

fluke.e: Unknown, perhaps dialectal. It seems to have originally referred to a lucky shot at billiards.
fluke.x: We've classified by a fluke; actually, the first goal was just a total fluke.

flunk.e: Alteration of funk, or perhaps a blend of flinch + funk.
flunk.x: Unsatisfied with Fred's progress, the teacher flunked him.

fluorescent.x: The fluorescent plants shimmered in the darkness.

fluoride.x: However, too much fluoride produces a mottling effect on teeth. Large doses of fluoride are actually toxic.

flurry.e: Perhaps an American English blend of flutter and hurry. Alternatively, perhaps from an obsolete term flurr (“scatter”).
flurry.x: "I missed the beast in my flurry, but he dropped you all right and was off like a streak."

flute.e: From Middle English fleute, floute, flote, from Old French flaute, fleüte, from Old Provençal flaüt, of uncertain origin.
flute.x: The group played huge drums placed overhead, along with flutes and a kotolike zither.

flyby.x: The upcoming flyby of Halley's comet is expected to provide new information on the nature of the comet.

flycatcher.x: The flies worried me when I was writing the other day. I put up a vampire flycatcher on my desk. One stuck to it, and I watched it struggling.

flyer.e: From fly + -er (agent noun suffix). With regard to the sense "female kangaroo": because of the high speed at which they move.

fodder.x: The sheep for fodder follow the shepherd, the shepherd for food follows not the sheep.

foehn.x: The foehn and the sun must have awakened the spirits of spring way up in the heights.

foggy.e: From fog + -y, originally in the sense "covered with tall grass; marshy; thick".

folder.x: I keep all my schoolwork in a yellow folder.

foliage.e: From earlier foilage, from Late Middle English ffoylage, from Middle French feuillage. The more recent form is influenced by Latin folium (“leaf”).

folklore.x: Crossing the ridge she stood at last upon the brink of Kor-ul-GRYF—the horror place of the folklore of her race.

follicle.x: He could feel the follicles in his inner ear go crazy.

follower.e: From Middle English folwer, folwere, folewer, from Old English folgere (“follower; attendant; disciple”), equivalent to follow + -er.
follower.x: I have over 50 followers on Twitter, but all my tweets only get 10 likes.

folly.e: Inherited from Middle English folie, from Old French folie (“madness”), from the adjective fol (“mad, insane”).
folly.x: It would be folly to walk all that way, knowing the shops are probably shut by now.

foment.e: From Middle English fomenten, a borrowing from Old French fomenter, from Late Latin fōmentāre, from Latin fōmentum (“lotion”), from fovēre (“heat, cherish”).
foment.x: He was arrested for fomenting a riot; after all, it's bad enough being in a riot but starting one is much worse.

fondue.e: Unadapted borrowing from French fondue (“melted”), from fondre (“to melt”).

fontanelle.e: Borrowed from French fontanelle, from Old French fontenelle, a diminutive of fontaine (“fountain, spring”) + -elle, from Late Latin fontāna, from Latin fontānus, from…

foolhardy.e: From Middle English folehardy, foolhardi, folherdi, from Old French fol hardi (“foolishly bold”), from Old French fol (“foolish, silly.

foolishness.e: From Middle English folishnesse, follissnesse, equivalent to foolish + -ness.

foosball.e: From German Fußball, itself a calque of English football.

footballer.e: From football + -er. For the kyphosid sense, named for the resemblance of their stripes to football uniforms.
footballer.x: It is footballers though, rather than commentators, presenters or pundits, who when interviewed have provided some of the best Colemanballs.

footbridge.e: From Middle English fot-brigge, equivalent to foot + bridge.
footbridge.x: The girder bridge at the head of the pass is used as a footbridge, and is roughly decked.

footpath.e: From Middle English foot path, footpath; equivalent to foot + path.

footprint.x: “Yes, there are two distinct sets of footprints, both wearing rubber shoes—one I think ordinary plimsolls, the other goloshes,” replied the sergeant.

footstep.e: From Middle English fotstep, fotstappe, from Old English *fōtstepe, *fōtstæpe (attested only in derivative fōtstappel (“footstep”)), equivalent to foot + step.
footstep.x: The child watched as his footsteps in the sand were washed away by the waves.

foray.e: From Middle English forrayen (“to pillage”), a back-formation of forrayour, forreour, forrier (“raider, pillager”), from Old French forrier, fourrier, a derivative of…

forbearance.x: Tut, tut, here is a mannerly forbearance: / The truth appeares ſo naked on my ſide, / That any purblind eye may find it out.

forcibly.e: From Middle English forceably, equivalent to forcible + -ly.

forearm.e: From fore- + arm. Compare Dutch voorarm (“forearm”), Danish forarm (“forearm”), German Vorderarm (“forearm”).

forebear.e: Late 15th century, from fore- + beer (“one who is or exists”, literally “be-er”).

foreboding.e: From Middle English forbodyng, vorboding, equivalent to fore- + bode + -ing. Compare German Vorbote (“harbinger, omen”).
foreboding.x: A sense of foreboding, the like of which he had never known before, hung heavily on him.

forecast.e: From Middle English forecasten, forcasten, equivalent to fore- + cast. The noun is from Middle English forecast, forcast.
forecast.x: This year alone, Japan is forecasted to install solar panels with the capacity of five to seven modern nuclear reactors.

forecastle.e: From Middle English forecastel, forcastel, (whence also Anglo-French forechasteil), equivalent to fore- + castle. Compare Dutch voorkasteel.

foreclosure.e: From foreclose by analogy with closure, equivalent to fore- + closure.

forefather.e: From Middle English forefader, forfader, vorvader, from Old English forefæder (“forefather”), but possibly also merged with Old Norse forfaðir.

forefinger.e: Mid-15th century, from Middle English forefynger; equivalent to fore- + finger.

foreground.e: From fore- + ground. Compare Dutch voorgrond (“foreground”), German Vordergrund (“foreground”), Danish forgrund (“foreground”), Swedish förgrund (“foreground”), Norwegian…

forehead.e: From Middle English forhed, forheed, from Old English forehēafod, from Proto-West Germanic *forēhaubid, corresponding to fore- + head.

foreigner.e: From Middle English forner, foreyner, foroner, forenere, augmentation of earlier forein (“foreigner”), from the adjective. Equivalent to foreign + -er.
foreigner.x: For a student of American history and a foreigner like myself, it is easier to understand all these extremisms of conscience.

forelock.e: From Middle English *forelock, *forelok, from Old English forelocc, equivalent to fore- + lock.

foreman.e: From Middle English foremon, forman. Compare West Frisian foarman, Dutch voorman, German Vormann, Danish formand, Swedish förman, Icelandic formaður.

foremost.x: She prankes not by hir mistresse side, she preases not to bée / The foremost of the companie, as when she erst was frée.

forerunner.e: From Middle English forrenner, foreriner. Calque of Latin praecursor (“one who runs before, a forerunner”). Equivalent to fore- + runner and/or forerun + -er.
forerunner.x: Bakelite is a forerunner of today's plastics.

foresee.e: From Middle English foreseen, forseen, from Old English foresēon; equivalent to fore- + see.
foresee.x: "I foresee in this," he says, "the breaking up of our profession."

foreseeable.x: This project will not be finished in the foreseeable future.

foresight.e: From Middle English forsight, forsyght, forsichte (since 14th c.), a calque of Latin providentia. By surface analysis, fore- + sight.
foresight.x: Having the foresight to prepare an evacuation plan may have saved their lives.

foreskin.e: From fore- + skin, a loose calque of Latin praepūtium. Compare German Vorhaut, etc. First attested in c. 1535.
foreskin.x: In the female genitalia, the clitoral hood is homologous to the foreskin.

forestall.e: From Middle English forestallen (“to forestall, intercept, ambush, way-lay”), from forestalle (“a forestalling, interception”), from Old English foresteall…
forestall.x: Fred forestalled disaster by his prompt action.

forested.x: Tasikoki has some 70 crested black macaques housed together in large, forested enclosures to let them establish hierarchies.

forester.e: Inherited from Middle English forester, a borrowing from Old French forestier, from forest + -ier; equivalent to forest + -er. Displaced native Old English wuduweard.

forestry.e: From Middle English *forestrie, *forsterie (suggested by Middle English forster, forester (“forester”)), from Old French foresterie, from forest.
forestry.x: She studied forestry and environmental management.

foretaste.e: From Middle English fortaste, equivalent to fore- + taste (noun).
foretaste.x: About two weeks ago I had another foretaste of success and immediately on it a veritable disaster.

foretell.e: First use appears before 1400, from Middle English foretellen, equivalent to fore- + tell.
foretell.x: Prodigies, foretelling the future eminence and lustre of his character.

foreword.e: Morphologically fore- + word. Calque of German Vorwort, itself a calque of Latin praefatio (“preface”).

forfeit.e: From Middle English forfait from ca. 1300, from Old French forfait (“crime”), originally the past participle of forfaire (“to transgress”), and Medieval Latin foris…
forfeit.x: He who murders pays the forfeit of his own life.

forge.e: From Middle English forge, from Old French forge, early Old French faverge, from Latin fabrica (“workshop”), from faber (“workman in hard materials, smith”) (genitive…
forge.x: In the greater bodies the forge was easy.

forger.e: From Middle English forger, forgere, from Old French forgiere; equivalent to forge + -er.

forgery.e: Recorded since 1574; from forge + -ery, from Middle English forgen, via Anglo-Norman forger, from Old French forgier, from Latin fabricārī (“to frame, construct…

forgetful.e: From Middle English *forgetful, *forȝetful (suggested by derivative forgetfulnesse, forȝetfulnesse (“forgetfulness”)), equivalent to forget + -ful.

forgetfulness.e: From Middle English forgetfulnes, forgetfulnesse, forȝetfulnesse, equivalent to forgetful + -ness.

forgo.e: From Middle English forgon (“to go by, pass up”), from Old English forgān (“to go away, forgo”); equivalent to for- + go.
forgo.x: I've had to forgo my student discount in exchange for taking the job.

forint.e: From Hungarian forint, from Italian fiorino (“florin, the former currency of Tuscany”). Doublet of florin.

forkful.x: He uncovered the fragrant eggs and b., and I pronged a moody forkful.

forlorn.e: From Middle English forlorn, forloren, from Old English forloren (past participle of forlēosan (“to lose”)), from Proto-Germanic *fraluzanaz (“lost”), past participle of…
forlorn.x: For here forlorn and loſt I tread, / With fainting ſteps and ſlow; / Where wilds immeaſurably ſpread, / Seem lengthening as I go.

formality.e: From Middle French formalité. equivalent to formal + -ity.
formality.x: The examination for priesthood is no mere formality, so we have to study well.

formation.e: From Middle English formacioun, formation, borrowed from Old French formacion, from Latin fōrmātiō, from fōrmō (“form”, verb); see form as verb.
formation.x: Some cloud formation was confirmed and rainfall was observed over some islands.

formerly.x: Xenia Robertson, formerly known as Xenia Isaamov, is from Ukraine.

formidable.e: From Middle English formidable, from Old French formidable, formible, from Latin formīdābilis (“formidable, terrible”) (whence -able), from formīdō (“fear, dread”).

formulation.x: The formulation with the bare infinitive was somewhat less common.

fornicate.e: First attested in 1552; borrowed from Latin fornicātus, perfect active participle of fornicor (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from fornix (“arch, vault; brothel”).

fornication.e: From Middle English fornicacioun, from Old French fornicacion, from Latin fornicātiō, from fornix (“brothel”).
fornication.x: FRIAR BARNARDINE. Thou hast committed— BARABAS. Fornication: but that was in another country; And besides, the wench is dead.

forsake.e: From Middle English forsaken (“to abandon, desert, repudiate, withdraw allegiance from”), from Old English forsacan (“to oppose; to give up, renounce.

forsythia.e: From New Latin, named in honor of Scottish horticulturist William Forsyth, who brought the shrub over from China.

forte.e: Borrowed 1640–50; earlier fort < Middle French; disyllabic pronunciation by association with Italian forte, from Latin fortis (“strong”). Doublet of fort and fortis.
forte.x: He writes respectably, but poetry is not his forte.

forthwith.e: From Middle English forth-with (“at once, immediately; at the same time, already.
forthwith.x: So he decreed, in words succinct, / That all who flirted, leered or winked, / (Unless connubially linked), / Should forthwith be beheaded.

fortification.e: Borrowed from Middle French fortification, from Late Latin fortificatio, fortificationem, from fortifico, from Latin fortis. By surface analysis, fort + -ification.

fortify.e: From Late Middle English fortifien, fortfien (“to strengthen (a castle, etc.) from attack; to strengthen (an army, etc.); to strengthen (a person), aid, support.
fortify.x: So pride came to the aid of fancy, and both combined to fortify his resolution to buy the estate if possible.

fortnight.e: From Middle English fourtenyght, fourtene nyght, from Old English fēowertīene niht (literally “fourteen nights".

fortress.e: Early 14 c., from Old French forteresce, forteresse, forterece (“strong place, fortification”), variant of fortelesse, from Medieval Latin fortalitia, from Latin fortis…
fortress.x: Like the Mesolithic age of 10,000-8000 B.C., the period 6000-4000 B.C. seems to be one of the fall of fortresses and the rise of pastoral nomadism.

fortuitous.e: Learned borrowing from Latin fortuītus (“happening by chance, accidental, random, fortuitous”), from *fortu- (“chance, fortune, luck”) + -ītus (suffix forming…
fortuitous.x: Was it love, she wondered, or a mere fortuitous combination of happy thoughts and sensations?

fortunate.e: From Middle English fortunat(e) (“fortunate”), from Latin fortūnātus, from fortūna (“fortune, luck”) + -ātus (adjective-forming suffix), see -ate (adjective-forming…
fortunate.x: We were fortunate not to be fined for speeding.

forum.e: From Latin forum (“public market place, forum”). Doublet of fuero and door.
forum.x: Trish was an admin on three forums, and had no trouble at all when it came to moderating them.

fossil.x: He draws eclectically on studies of baboons, descriptive anthropological accounts of hunter-gatherer societies and, in a few cases, the fossil record.

founder.e: From Middle French fondrer (“send to the bottom”), from Latin fundus (“bottom”).
founder.x: The founder of Facebook is Mark Zuckerberg.

foundling.e: From Middle English foundlyng, fondeyng, variants of Middle English fyndling, fyndlyng. By surface analysis, found + -ling.
foundling.x: In foundling hospitals, and among the children brought up by parish charities, the mortality is still greater than among those of the common people.

foundry.e: From French fonderie. By surface analysis, found (“to melt (metals)”) + -ry (“place; process”).

fountain.x: His house is right beside that fountain on Street 15.

fourteenth.e: Inherited from Middle English fourtenthe, fourtethe, from Old English fēowertēoþa, equivalent to fourteen + -th.

foxhole.e: From Middle English foxhol, from Old English foxhol, equivalent to fox + hole.

foxtail.e: Inherited from Middle English fox-tail. By surface analysis, fox + tail.
foxtail.x: Look at the foxtails growing along the road.

foyer.e: Borrowed from French foyer (“hearth, lobby”), in turn from Vulgar Latin *focārium, from Late Latin focārius, from Latin focus (“hearth”).
foyer.x: We had a drink in the foyer waiting for the play to start.

fractal.e: From French fractal, from Latin fractus (“broken”), perfect passive participle of frangō (“break, fragment”).

fraction.x: Gasoline prices show the mill as a fraction, for example $3.59+⁹⁄₁₀.

fragile.e: Borrowed from Middle French fragile, from Latin fragilis, formed on frag-, the root of frangere (“to break”). Cognate with fraction, fracture and doublet of frail.
fragile.x: She caught the fragile vase before it could shatter on the floor.

fragility.e: Borrowed from Middle French fragilité, from Latin fragilitās. Doublet of frailty. Morphologically fragile + -ity.

fragment.e: From Late Middle English fragment, from Latin fragmentum (“a fragment, remnant”), from frangō (“to break”) + -mentum.
fragment.x: I heard a small fragment of the conversation.

fragmentary.x: Fragmentary evidence suggests that he died in a foreign country.

fragrant.e: Borrowed from Latin frāgrāns, present active participle of frāgrō (“to smell”).
fragrant.x: party-political interventions made by the fragrant Ms Stella Rimington.

frail.e: From Middle English frele, fraill, from Old French fraile, from Latin fragilis. Cognate to fraction, fracture, and doublet of fragile.
frail.x: Frail smoke of morning in the air and a sort of muffled hum that is not sound but is not silence either.

frailty.e: From Middle English frelete, frailte, from Old French fraileté, from Latin fragilitās. By surface analysis, frail + -ty. Doublet of fragility.

framework.x: These ‘three principles of connexion’ compose the framework of principles in Hume's account of the association of ideas.

franchise.e: From Middle English franchise, fraunchise, from Old French franchise (“freedom”), a derivative of franc (“free”). More at frank.

frangipani.e: From French frangipane, from Italian frangipane. Possibly named after Muzio Frangipane, a 16th-century marquess of the Italian noble Frangipani family, who invented a…

frankincense.e: From Old French franc encens (“noble incense”).
frankincense.x: “Flame-coloured are his wings, and coloured like flame is his body. His lips are sweet as honey, and his breath is like frankincense.”

frantic.e: From Middle English frantike, frentik, variant of frenetik, from Old French frenetique, from Late Latin phreneticus, alteration of phreniticus, from φρενιτικός…
frantic.x: They returned the missing child to his frantic mother.

fraternal.e: PIE word *bʰréh₂tēr Borrowed from Middle French fraternel, from Medieval Latin frāternālis (“fraternal”), from Latin frāternus (“of or pertaining to a brother…
fraternal.x: Yet, in leaving, Judah removes himself not only from fraternal violence but from familial destiny as well.

fraternity.e: PIE word *bʰréh₂tēr From Middle English fraternite, borrowed from Old French fraternité, from Latin frāternitās, ultimately from frāter (“brother”).

fratricide.e: From Middle French fratricide or its etymon Latin frātricīdium.
fratricide.x: Such a press of arms invites many opportunities for unintentional fratricide.

fraudulent.e: From Middle English fraudulent, from Old French fraudulent, from Latin fraudulentus, from fraus (“fraud”).
fraudulent.x: He tried to pass a fraudulent check.

freckle.e: The noun is derived from Late Middle English fracle, frekel, frekle (“freckle; pimple; fleck of colour in a stone”), a variant of frakne, freken (“freckle.
freckle.x: Steve has brown hair, blue eyes, and freckles on his cheeks and nose.

freckled.e: Inherited from Middle English frekled; equivalent to freckle + -ed.
freckled.x: A smile grew across Jim's freckled face.

freefall.x: SAC has a bomber study currently in progress to see how many freefalls, how many SRAM, how many ALCM's they need to fill out the force.

freelance.x: The person you are revising (the revisee) is a colleague at your own rank, or another freelance.

freezer.x: The packinghouse usually delivers shrimp to a few regular customers, such as breaders, freezers, canners, or wholesalers of fresh shrimp.

freight.x: The freight shifted and the trailer turned over on the highway.

frenetic.e: From Middle English frenetik (also frentik, frentyk, frantike > modern English frantic), from Old French frenetike, from Latin phreneticus, from Ancient Greek φρενητικός…
frenetic.x: After a week of working at a frenetic pace, she was ready for Saturday.

frequency.e: From Latin frequentia, from frequens. By surface analysis, frequent + -cy.
frequency.x: With growing confidence, the Viking’s raids increased in frequency.

frequent.e: From Old French frequent, from Latin frequens (“crowded, crammed, frequent, repeated, etc.”), possibly from a Proto-Indo-European *bʰrekʷ- (“to cram together”).
frequent.x: I take frequent breaks so I don't get too tired.

frequently.x: He was enrolled but frequently didn't attend class.

fresco.e: From Italian fresco, from Vulgar Latin *friscum, from Proto-Germanic *friskaz. Doublet of fresh and frisk.

freshwater.x: Lake Baikal is the world's largest freshwater lake in terms of volume.

friable.e: Borrowed from French friable, from Latin friābilis (“friable”), from friō (“to crumble”).
friable.x: This light, friable type of material offered excellent insulation against both desert heat and also the cold of darkness during the winter.

friction.e: From Middle French friction and directly from Latin frictionem, nom. frictio (“a rubbing, rubbing down”).
friction.x: Users have reported friction from having to enter their passwords many times a day.

friendless.e: From Middle English frendles, from Old English frēondlēas. By surface analysis, friend + -less.

friendliness.e: From Middle English freendlynesse, frendlynes, equivalent to friendly + -ness.

frieze.e: Late Middle English, from French and Middle French frise, probably from Medieval Latin Frisia (“Frisian (wool)”) due to import via Northern ships.
frieze.x: From beggar's frieze to monarch's robe, / One common doom is pass'd; / Sweet nature's works, the swelling globe, / Must all burn out at last.

frigate.e: From French frégate, from Italian fregata, of uncertain origin.

fright.e: From Middle English fright, furht, from Old English fryhtu, fyrhto (“fright, fear, dread, trembling, horrible sight”), from Proto-Germanic *furhtį̄ (“fear”), from…

frighten.e: From Middle English *frightenen, equivalent to fright + -en.
frighten.x: Avery puts a sheet over her head, pretending to be a ghost to frighten Emily.

frightening.x: Riding the rollercoaster was a frightening experience.

frightful.e: From Middle English frightful (“afraid”), from Old English forhtfull (“fainthearted, timorous”). Equivalent to fright + -ful.

frigid.x: In Italy, a plant called Pizza ugurdu is said to excite powerful erotic feelings even in the most frigid.

fringe.e: From Middle English frenge, from Old French frenge, from Vulgar Latin *frimbia, a metathesis of Latin fimbriae (“fibers, threads, fringe”, plural), of uncertain origin.
fringe.x: The walls were hung with blue silk, edged with silver fringe; and the closely-drawn blue velvet curtains swept the ground.

frisky.x: He had his hands full, with three frisky kittens in the house.

fritter.e: Inherited from Middle English fryture, from Middle French friture, from Old French friture, from Vulgar Latin *frīctūra, from Latin frīgō (“to fry”); compare fry.
fritter.x: And cut whole giants into fritters.

frivolous.e: From Latin frīvolus (“silly, empty, trifling, frivolous, worthless”), with the ending modified to match -ous.
frivolous.x: One of the major cost drivers in the delivery of health care are these junk and frivolous lawsuits.

frock.e: From Middle English frok, frokke, from Old French froc (“frock, a monk's gown or habit”), perhaps via Medieval Latin hrocus, roccus, rocus (“a coat”), from Frankish…

frogman.e: From frog + man, due to the fact that frogs are amphibious.

frolic.e: From Dutch vrolijk (“cheerful”), from Middle Dutch vrolijc, from Old Dutch frōlīk, from Proto-Germanic *frawalīkaz.

frontal.e: Borrowed from New Latin frontālis, from frons (“the forehead, brow, front”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix), equivalent to front + -al; cognate of French frontal.

frontier.e: From Middle English frounter, from Old French fronter (whence Modern French frontière), from front.
frontier.x: For two years the Easterner had been searching for his lost brother, at trading posts and Army forts all along the frontier.

frost.x: Thus I was; in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep departed from mine eyes.

frosty.e: From Middle English frosty, forsty, from Old English forstiġ, fyrstiġ (“frosty”), from Proto-West Germanic *frostag, *frustīg, By surface analysis, frost + -y.
frosty.x: The air was frosty; I could see my breath and walked quickly with my hands in my pockets.

froth.e: From Middle English froth, frooth, froþ, likely a borrowing from Old Norse froða, from Proto-Germanic *fruþǭ.
froth.x: Thousands of African children die each day: why do the newspapers continue to discuss unnecessary showbiz froth?

frothy.x: I like my milkshakes frothy, not flat like this!

frown.e: From Middle English frown, froun (“a threatening appearance; lowering of the clouds”), from frounen (“to frown”). See below.
frown.x: He encounters some obstacle in his train of reasoning ... and then a frown passes like a shadow over his brow.

frugal.e: From Middle French, from Latin frugalis (“virtuous, thrifty”). Displaced native Old English spærhende (literally “spare-handed”).

frugality.e: Borrowed from Middle French frugalité. By surface analysis, frugal + -ity.
frugality.x: With the frugality that hard graft begets, his mate limited both his and her own tobacco, so he must not smoke all afternoon.

fruitcake.e: Compound of fruit + cake. First attested in c. 1687. Sense 2, predated by nutty as a fruitcake, was first attested in c. 1952.

fruitful.e: From Middle English fruitefull, equivalent to fruit + -ful. Compare Dutch vruchtvol, German fruchtvoll, Swedish fruktfull.
fruitful.x: And God blessed them, saying, Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let fowl multiply in the earth.

fruitless.e: Inherited from Middle English fruytles; equivalent to fruit + -less. Compare Middle English withouten fruyt (“fruitless”, literally “without fruit”).
fruitless.x: The unskilled man’s attempt at fixing his car engine was fruitless.

fruity.x: That moist and fruity dish is simply delectable.

frustrate.e: From Middle English frustraten (“to prevent, disappoint, render useless”), from Latin frūstrātus, perfect passive participle of frūstrō (“to deceive”), see -ate…
frustrate.x: My clumsy fingers frustrate my typing efforts.

frustration.e: From Latin frūstrātiō (“disappointment”), related to frūstrā (“in vain”). By surface analysis, frustrate + -ion.

fuchsia.x: She tilted a hand topped with long rectangular nails in furious fuchsia towards her cheeks and fluttered the fingers, fanning.

fudge.e: Probably a variant of fadge (“to fit”), the confectionery sense having evolved from the meaning of “merging together” or “turning out as expected”.
fudge.x: Have you tried the vanilla fudge? It's delicious!

fugitive.x: I found afterwards that he was the chauffeur, who filled the gaps left by a succession of fugitive butlers.

fugue.e: Borrowed from French fugue, from Italian fuga (“flight, ardor”), from Latin fuga (“act of fleeing”), from fugiō (“to flee”); compare Ancient Greek φυγή (phugḗ).
fugue.x: Jacobsen's theory about the empty storehouse is still valid, for a myth never has one meaning only; a myth is a polyphonic fugue of many voices.

fulcrum.e: Borrowed from Latin fulcrum (“bedpost, foot of a couch”), from fulciō (“prop up, support”).
fulcrum.x: It is possible to flick food across the table using your fork as a lever and your finger as a fulcrum.

fulfill.e: From Middle English fulfillen, from Old English fullfyllan (“to fill full”). By surface analysis, full- + fill.
fulfill.x: You made a promise, son, and now you must fulfill it.

fulfilment.e: From Middle English fulfillen, from Old English fullfyllan, from full (“full”) + fyllan (“to fill”). Equivalent to fulfill + -ment.
fulfilment.x: To achieve fulfilment of one's hopes.

fuller.e: Inherited from Middle English fullere, from Old English fullere, from Latin fullō (“fuller”) + -ere; equivalent to full (“to densen cloth”) + -er.

fullness.e: From Middle English fulnesse, from Old English fulnes, fylnes, fyllnis (“completeness; abundance”), equivalent to full + -ness.
fullness.x: The actor enjoyed the fullness of his success.

fumarole.e: Borrowed from Italian fumarola. Likely a doublet of femerell. By surface analysis, fume + -ar + -ola.

fumble.e: From late Middle English, from Low German fummeln, fommeln, fammeln (German fummeln), or Dutch fommelen. Or, perhaps from a Scandinavian/North Germanic source.
fumble.x: Waiting for the interview, he fumbled with his tie.

fumigate.e: First attested in 1530; borrowed from Latin fūmigātus, perfect passive participle of fūmigō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from fūmus (“smoke”).

functional.x: That sculpture is not merely artistic, but also functional: it can be used as a hatrack.

functionary.e: From French fonctionnaire; by surface analysis, function + -ary.

fundamental.x: Personal leadership is a fundamental of successful government.

fundamentalism.e: From fundamental + -ism. First used in the 1910s by American Christians.

fundamentalist.e: From fundamental + -ist, after a book series called “The Fundamentals: A Testimony to the Truth“ (1910).

funding.x: However the collapse in demand for rail and air travel caused by the pandemic has had a knock-on effect for the project's funding.

funerary.e: Borrowed from Late Latin fūnerārius, from Latin funus.

funereal.e: From Middle French funerail, from Latin funereus + -al.
funereal.x: Seven were chosen to push the funereal boat to the water, in honor of the seven faces of god.

fungal.x: Doctors determined that the cause of the itchy rash was fungal rather than bacterial.

fungus.e: Borrowed from Latin fungus (“mushroom”). Displaced native Old English swamm.

funicular.e: From Latin fūniculus (“thinner cord”), diminutive from fūnis (“rope, cord”) + -culus. By surface analysis, funicul(us) + -ar.

funnel.e: From Middle English funell, fonel, probably through Old French *founel (compare Middle French fonel, Old Occitan fonilh, enfounilh), from Latin fundibulum, infundibulum…

furlong.e: PIE word *dlongʰos From Middle English furlong, forlong (“unit of distance about one-eighth of a mile; quantity of land equal to one square furlong.
furlong.x: The fresh and desperate onset bore / The foes three furlongs back and more, / Leaving their noblest in their gore.

furlough.e: From Dutch verlof (“furlough”), probably from Middle Low German verlōf (“furlough, permission”) (possibly via German Verlaub), from the verb verlōven (“to allow”), from…
furlough.x: And I had a lot of things on my mind and I pretty well forgot my promise to Mama until I got shipped home on a special furlough for her funeral.

furnish.e: From Middle English furnysshen, from Old French furniss-, stem of certain parts of furnir, fornir (Modern French fournir), from Germanic, from Frankish *frumjan (“to…
furnish.x: The resin-coated furnish is evenly spread inside the form and another metal plate is placed on top.

furrow.x: Don't walk across that deep furrow in the field.

furry.x: His treatment of our furry friends was nothing short of appalling.

furthermore.e: From Middle English furthermore, forthermore, forthermar (also as forther mo), equivalent to further + -more.
furthermore.x: He skillfully took charge of the event, and furthermore, he stayed late after it to clean up.

furtive.e: From Middle English *furtyve (implied in furtyvely (adverb)), from Middle French furtif, furtive (“furtive, stealthy”) (modern French furtif), from Latin fūrtīvus…
furtive.x: I noticed the same singular, and as it were, furtive glance over the shoulder that had attracted my attention in the Cassino.

fusilli.e: From Italian fusilli, plural of fusillo, diminutive of fuso (“spindle”).
fusilli.x: Fusilli is very good served with classic tomato sauces.

fusion.e: First appears c. 1555, in a translation by Richard Eden. From Middle French fusion, from Latin fūsiōnem (the accusative of fūsiō), from fusus, past participle of fundō…

fussy.x: The internal decor of the SR-built Bulleid corridor stock was noticeably cleaner and less fussy than that of prewar coaches.

futile.e: Borrowed from Middle French futile, from Latin fūtilis.
futile.x: He wished he had not been saddled with Whippham's rather futile son as his chaplain.

futility.e: From Latin fūtilitās (“worthlessness, futility”). By surface analysis, futile + -ity.
futility.x: His taking the bar exam for a third time was pure futility.

futon.e: Borrowed from Japanese 布団 (futon), in turn from Middle Chinese 蒲團 (MC bu dwan, “meditation cushion”) (compare Mandarin 蒲团 (pútuán)), from 蒲 (bu, “bulrush, cattail”) + 團…
futon.x: The futon are easily aired, and may be carried about readily when moving.
